doc.title: Jonathan Scales interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 23, 2025

title: Note layouts and sticking on the pans
summary: Tenor pans use circles of fourths or fifths, double seconds whole-tone layouts, guitars and cellos diminished chords.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Okay that makes sense. I wonder then if on the tenor pans if you’re playing a descending chromatic line for instance. Is it a left-right-left-right to get those notes?

Okay so each of these sets of pans have their own different – I don’t want to say standardization but like a rough general thing. So like tenor pans are set up in a circle of fourths, or a circle of fifths. So if you have a C right here then you have a G right beside it, then you have a D, then you have an A, then you have an E. So it’s literally set up in a circle of fifths. The other way would be fourths. C, F, B flat. You know? The pans I play, which are called the double seconds, they’re actually set up in whole tone scales. So half of my notes are on one side. So for me chromatically it is left-right-left-right. But the patterns within that are not symmetrical because of the way the notes are arranged within – it’s not in any straight line or any spiral or anything like that on the double seconds. You know the guitars and the cellos are set up in diminished – they have – like within one drum you have the diminished chords. You see what I’m saying?
